title: Becoming a Dungeon Master
contentHtml:
Running your first game as a Dungeon Master can feel daunting, but it's one of the most rewarding creative experiences you can have. You're not just telling a story — you're building a world that responds to your players' choices.

Start Small

You don't need a sprawling continent with a thousand years of history. A single village, a nearby dungeon, and one looming threat is enough to run a great session.

The Three Pillars

Every good D&D session balances:

  • Exploration — letting players discover the world
  • Social interaction — roleplaying with NPCs
  • Combat — tactical, dramatic encounters

Lean into whichever pillar your table enjoys most, but don't neglect the others entirely.

Preparation vs. Improvisation

Prepare situations, not scripts. If you know what the villain wants and what the world looks like now, you can improvise everything else on the fly.

title: Building a Magic System for Your Fantasy World
contentHtml:
A magic system is one of the most defining features of a fantasy setting. Whether you're writing a novel or designing a campaign, a well-crafted system makes your world feel real.

Hard vs. Soft Magic

Hard magic has clear rules the reader (or player) can understand. Think of it like a science — predictable, with costs and limits.

Soft magic is mysterious and unexplained. It creates wonder and awe, but shouldn't be used to solve plot problems.

Most great fantasy settings use a mix of both — hard magic for the everyday, soft magic for the cosmic.

The Cost of Magic

Every good magic system has a cost. Ask yourself:

  1. What does casting a spell take from the caster?
  2. Who gets to use magic, and why?
  3. What happens when magic goes wrong?

The answers shape your world's politics, economy, and culture.

Magic Shapes Society

If teleportation exists, there are no trade caravans. If healing magic is common, there are no plagues. Let your magic ripple outward into every corner of your world.

title: Running a Session Zero for Your D&D Campaign
contentHtml:
Before the dice ever hit the table, the most important session of your campaign happens: Session Zero.

What Is Session Zero?

It's a meeting — sometimes a full session, sometimes just an hour — where the group discusses expectations, boundaries, and the shape of the game before it begins.

Topics to Cover

  • Tone — Is this a grimdark epic or a lighthearted romp?
  • Content boundaries — What themes are off-limits for your group?
  • Character concepts — How do the PCs know each other? Why do they adventure together?
  • House rules — Any homebrew, variant rules, or table conventions?
  • Scheduling — How often will you meet, and for how long?

Why It Matters

A good Session Zero prevents misaligned expectations down the road. It also gives everyone a chance to build characters that fit the world and each other, so session one starts with momentum instead of awkward introductions.

Treat it as seriously as any other session — it's the foundation the whole campaign sits on.
